'''''Hoya carnosa''''', the '''porcelain flower''' or '''wax plant''', is a [[species]] of [[flowering plant]] in the family [[Apocynaceae]], native to East Asia. It is a common [[house plant]] grown for its attractive waxy foliage, and sweetly scented flowers. It is grown well in pots and hanging baskets.

''Hoya carnosa'' has been in cultivation for more than 200 years and has given rise to many cultivars that vary in foliage form or flower color. In cultivation in the UK it has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref name = RHSPF>{{cite web | url= https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/8852/i-Hoya-carnosa-i/Details | title = RHS Plantfinder - ''Hoya carnosa''
| access-date=3 March 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite web  | url= https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants - Ornamental | date = July 2017 | page = 49 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | access-date = 2 March 2018}}</ref>

==Description==
''Hoya carnosa'' makes faintly succulent [[Shoot (botany)|shoots]] with smooth, pale gray, and bare surfaces that [[Vine#Twining vines|twine]] and [[vine|climb]]. The perennial leaves are wide oval to longitudinal oval or heart-shaped. They are slightly [[succulent]], fleshy with a waxy glossy surface, {{convert|3-5|cm}} wide and {{convert|3.5-13|cm}} long, with a [[petiole (botany)|petiole]] of about {{convert|1-1.5|cm}}. The spindle-shaped fruits measure 6 to 10 × 0.5 to 1.5 cm.<ref>Focke Albers, Ulli Meve (ed.): Succulent Encyclopedia. Asclepiadaceae (milkweed plants) . Eugen Ulmer, Stuttgart 2002, {{ISBN|3-8001-3982-0}} , p 150</ref>

===Flowers===
[[File:Hoya FR 2013.jpg|thumb|Flower]]
The [[inflorescence]] is made up of numerous flowers, hanging or more upright, which are grouped in an [[umbel]]. The flowers are typically light pink, but may vary from near-white to dark pink; they are star-shaped, and are borne in clusters. The thick flower [[Petal#Corolla|corollas]] look as if made from porcelaine or from wax, leading to the plant's common names. The surface of the flowers is covered in tiny hairs giving them a fuzzy sheen. They are heavily scented and may produce excess [[nectar]] that drips from the flowers. A single flower (corolla) has a diameter of 1.5 to 2 cm.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.plantoftheweek.org/week029.shtml |title=Hoya carnosa - Wax Plant, Asclepiadaceae |website=Plant of The Week |date=May 1999 |publisher=University of Oklahoma Department of Microbiology & Plant Biology |access-date=December 6, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080417091309/http://www.plantoftheweek.org/week029.shtml |archive-date=April 17, 2008 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

Like most species of ''Hoya'', ''H. carnosa'' flowers grow from specialised perennial [[Peduncle (botany)|peduncles]]; sometimes these structures are referred to as [[Spur (stem)|spurs]]. These appear from the axils of the leaves and stem; flowers may not be produced when the spurs first appear, but in time [[bud]]s emerge from their tips. New flowers are produced on these same spurs every year, so they should not be removed.

The plant flowers from spring to late summer, it can produce umbels of 10 to 50 small star-shaped flowers that mature gradually (2 to 3 weeks) on the same peduncle. The scent is nocturnal with a [[pheromone|pheromonal]] tendency.
{{clear}}

==Distribution and habitat==
''Hoya carnosa'' is native to [[southern China]] (including [[Hainan]]), [[Taiwan]], [[Laos]] and Japan (including the [[Ryukyu Islands]]).<ref name=POWO/>

== Cultivation ==
''Hoya carnosa'' prefers indirect bright light, but will tolerate much less. Though it will tolerate low temperatures (but not freezing),<ref name=RHSPF/> the optimal temperature is {{convert|60|-|85|°F|°C}}. It can be propagated by [[air layering]] or by stem cuttings. It benefits from an open potting medium that allows some air to get to the roots. Typical mixes include large-grade drainage material such as [[perlite]], [[pumice]], or [[ceramic]] balls. The plants should be fed regularly with a fertilizer suitable for epiphytic plants.

There is a persistent piece of belief that hoyas prefer to be pot-bound (kept in a small pot). It is said that this will hasten flowering.<ref>{{Cite web| title = Hoya Plant: How To Care For The Wax Plant| work = Plant Care Today| access-date = 2017-06-07| date = 2016-05-26| url = https://plantcaretoday.com/how-to-care-for-grow-and-bloom-hoya-plants.html}}</ref>

Studies at the [[University of Georgia]], published in 2009, have shown ''H. carnosa'' to be an excellent remover of pollutants in the indoor environment.<ref name=UGA>{{cite web |url=http://www.uga.edu/about_uga/profile/some-plants-remove-indoor-pollutants/ |title=UGA research shows some plants can remove indoor pollutants |website=UGA.edu |date=March 31, 2009 |publisher=University of Georgia |access-date=December 6, 2015}}</ref>

=== ''‘Compacta’'' ===

[[File:Hoya compacta 18.JPG|right|thumb|''Hoya carnosa ‘Compacta’'' <ref>{{Cite web |title=Hoya compacta C.M.Burton {{!}} Plants of the World Online {{!}} Kew Science |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:940449-1 |access-date=2025-05-19 |website=Plants of the World Online |language=en}}</ref>]]
The cultivar ''Hoya carnosa ‘Compacta’,'' was first discovered as a branch mutation [[Sport (botany)|sport]] at Hummel’s Exotic Gardens of [[Inglewood, California]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Drysdale |first=William |date=April 1, 1992 |title=Hoyas: A Personal View |journal=The Hoyan |volume=13 |issue=4 |pages=59–60}}</ref> and is characterized by its folded, curled leaves and tight internodal spacing, growing in the form of a rope.

It was later popularized in 1967 under the trademark “Hindu Rope” by B. L. Cobia Nursery Inc. of [[Winter Garden, Florida]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Cobia |first=Barnell |date=April 1, 1967 |title=Hindu Rope - #72252947 |url=https://tsdr.uspto.gov/#caseNumber=72252947&caseSearchType=US_APPLICATION&caseType=DEFAULT&searchType=statusSearch |access-date=2025-05-19 |website=United States Patent and Trademark Office {{!}} tsdr.uspto.gov}}</ref>
